title: Long-format, wide-format, and wide-names
text:
Attribute naming exceptions
For combined attributes, the regular attribute formula (tableShortName_attribute) becomes
tableShortName_n_aggregation_attribute1_..._attributeN
Where n is an integer indicating the number of attributes being combined together, the aggregation is a boolean aggregation of either OR or AND to indicate whether the column records all of the attribute, or one or another. Finally, the attributes are listed in snake case. This wide-names is still machine readable.
For example, a wide-column name where sample collection period and collection number are reported together would be:
sm_2_AND_collPer_collNum
For _AND_ style wide-names, the default separator must be a period (.). So for the is example, where we are recording the sample collection period and number together, a value of a 24-hour period with 12 collections would be 24.12.

title: Long-format, wide-format, and wide-names
text:
Measure and method naming exceptions
For combined measures or methods, the ..._n_... approach is also used.
For measures, the formula is: compartment_specimen_fraction_n_aggregation(bool)_measure1_measure2_..._measureN_unit_aggregation_index_attribute, where all measures must share the same units and aggregation. For example, a column to measure the presence of “other” mutations, alleles, or variants uses the wide-name wat_sa_liq_3_OR_otherM_otherA_otherV_gcMl_m_value.
For Methods the use case is slightly more constrained. Protocol steps are rarely combined into a single field. Protocol steps using one or more measures which report a single value would be highly unlikely to exist. Protocol steps using methods combinations only work and make sense because the inputs are categorical and defined. The suggested structure for a protocol step using only methods (and no measures) would follow the formula tableShortName_partTypeShortName_n_aggregation_method1_..._methodN_attribute.
For example a column where one specifies the protocol step for either pcr or sequencing strategy in a wastewater program would be called ps_met_wat_sa_liq_2_OR_pcrmeth_seqStrat_value.
In instances of OR wide names, the values sets for the different measures or methods are distinct, and the sets information for the input can be used to determine which method or measure is being reported.

title: Long-format, wide-format, and wide-names
text:
Building a wide-format ODM headers
We’re going to transform an example long-format measure table to wide-format. In figure 5 we see the list of all the possible headers in the measures table. Not all of the headers are mandatory, so you may choose not to use them all. Our tutorial here is just to write out what the wide name would be for each of these headers.



Figure 5 - Headers in the Measures Table


Everything in this table is an attribute, except for (eventually) the value field. We know that attributes use the structure:
tableShortName_attribute
So with that in mind, see if you can type up or write out what you think the ODM wide name would be for all of these headers - skipping the value header. Keep in mind that for headers that are foreign keys (noted FK in figure 5), that the table short name used should be the table in which those attributes are a primary key. You may want to consult the ERD and the parts list to double check which tables host the primary keys and what the short names are for those tables.

title: Reference guide
text:
Dictionary v3.0.1 Documentation v2.1.1
The reference guide is a technical description of the ODM parts. There are three sections to the reference guide.

parts – Parts are the smallest way of describing anything in the ODM. An analogy to parts of a car can be used to illustrate this point. If you own a car, your garage can access a parts list that contains every part of your car, right down to every nut and bolt. There are over 2200 parts, all listed in alphabetical order. Each part has up to 60 different attributes such as the part name and description.
tables - The ODM database model has 26 tables in its full relational database. The full model is commonly referred to as “long” tables as it stores data with one measurement per row. The most important tables are the ‘report’ tables that are used for daily reporting of measures and samples.
sets - Sets are lists or collections of parts. You can think of sets as the elements of drop down lists or categories.







TipDid you know that each part ID has its own URL?



Every part, table, and set has its own URL, that is created using the partID. partIDs are usually parentheses that follow a part, table, or set name.
For example, ‘airport’ is a sample shed category which would appear as: Airport (airport). The permanent link to the airport partID is, https://docs.phes-odm.org/parts.html#airport. Airport also is listed in the Sampleshed category set (shedCatSet).

title: Parts
text:
Dictionary v3.0.1 Documentation v2.1.1
Parts are the smallest way of describing anything in the ODM. An analogy to parts of a car can be used to illustrate this point. If you own a car, your garage can access a parts list that contains every part of your car, right down to every nut and bolt. Similarly, the ODM has a part ID (partID) and part description (partDescription) for every measure, method, and attribute. There are also part IDs for units, aggregations, and other parts. The part list is presented below.






TipDid you know you can identify part IDs by their specific naming format?





Each part ID starts with a lowercase character and contains no special characters. Parts have less than 12 characters, while part types such as units and aggregations have a maximum of seven characters.
The unique construction of part IDs serves several purposes in addition to generating valid URLs. Users can create wide table variable names (headers) using part IDs that are valid in all open software languages. ODM supports a standard method of generating wide variable names by concatenating partIDs with an underscore, _. For this reason, some part types have a limit of seven characters to ensure the total length of wide names remains less than 35 characters, which is the character limit length of some statistical language software. Details on wide variable naming and standards can be found in the Long-format, wide-format, and wide-names section.

(derivedSamp). A sample that is derived or made from another sample or material. A derived sample is a type of sample created by mixing material obtained from a field sample (e.g., wastewater, soil, or air) with additional additives in a laboratory setting. This process can involve diluting the original field sample with clean water or other solutions, as needed. Derived samples are typically used to adjust the concentration of the target substance or organism, making it more suitable for analysis or to test the efficiency and sensitivity of detection methods. In the example given, a derived sample might be a sub-sample of wastewater that is diluted with clean water to achieve a specific concentration, allowing for more accurate and reliable analysis. (lastEdited). The date the entry was last updated. Use lastEdited if an entry is updated. Leave lastEdited blank or ‘NA’ for the first entry. Updates can include additions or revisions of the entry for any reason. For example, a wastewater measure was repeated later with an improved method. You can revise the entry by updating the value and then adding the date the new measure was performed to ‘lastEdited’. To ensure data provenance, the best practice in this example is to generate a new entry with the same measureID as the original measureID. The original and new measures are kept in the database with a date in the ‘lastEdited’ field for the new entry but not the original one. Some databases may choose a delete-and-replace approach where the original entry is deleted and replaced by a new entry. In this approach, the ‘lastEdited’ field indicates the delete and replace occurred. (partID). The unique identify of any entity within the dictionary. Every entity in the ODM has a partID. The partID must be unique with no duplcates. partIDs are short. partIDs that are constructed by different part attributes can be up 28 characters (check max), but each part attibute should be 1 to 5 characters. partIDs are machine readible, but a knowledgable user can understand what they represent. partID are used, for example, as a header in an Excel input table. Numbers are allowed but there no other special characters other than ``. `` is a reserved character that is used to generate a partID using a compoent or table attributes. A partID for a subComponent is automatically generated using attributes of a component. For example, the partID for the compoent `SARS-CoV-2` is `covid`. `Covid` can have many subComponents including different groups (Covid-19-al, Covid-19-va, ovid-pr (allele, variant or protein) or units and aggregatrions (i.e. covid-al-N1-mean-cpl representing ovid allele N1, mean observation of viral copies per litre of effluent). (recomb). A catch-all measure for viruses of non-specified and recombinant lineages, defined as those virsues wherein viruses of two different parent strains coinfect the same host cell and interact during replication to generate virus progeny that have some genes from both parents. Recombination generally occurs between members of the same virus type (e.g., between two influenza viruses or between two herpes simplex viruses). This is particularly common in the evolution of coronaviruses and sarbecoviruses. Please bundle with a more general pathogen measure in a common measure set, so that it is clear to what species the recombinant virus belongs. title: Sets
text:
NA
Dictionary v3.0.1 Documentation v2.1.1
Sets are lists of categories and other parts. For example, “Collection category set” (collectSet) (collectSet) contains a list of the different collection types including: mooreSw (Moore swab), grb (Grab sample), flowPr (Flow proportional sample), etc.
Sets can have parts that are reused. For example, there are different quality measures for sample collection (e.g. Sample not collected), PCR measures (Inhibition preset), and sequencing measures (Low depth of coverage), but all quality sets share the No quality concerns indicator.

NA (aggregations). Statistical measures used to report a measure. Each measure reported as a number should be reported with an aggregation. The default aggregation is sin, which corresponds to a single measurement. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (aggregationScales). The scale of an aggregation set. Aggregation scales include quantitative and qualitative. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (aggregationSets). Sets of aggregations. Examples of aggregation sets include logarithm, linear and boolean. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (attributes). Attributes describe the who, where, when, and why of environmental surveillance. There are attributes for domain, specimen, compartment, or table. Attributes are one of the three main components or ways to report environment surviellence data. The other two components are measures and methods. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (categories). A discrete list of values that can be reported for a measure, method or attribute. A use-case example of categories would be how they are used to record the site where a measure is taken (partID = geoType). For the geoType attribute there are different type of sites where samples can be taken: a wastwater treatment plant, airplane holding tank, wastwater pumping station, etc. Each of these site types is recorded as a category that can be identified in categorySetID = sTypeCatSets Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (classes). A class is a collection of one or more related measures or methods within a group. A group can have one more more classes to describe different parts or the class. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (compartments). The substance from which a sample was taken. For example, wastewater has component of “water”. Compartments are attributes of measures, methods, units, and aggregations. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (compartmentSets). Sets of compartments. Compartment sets are used to identify when a measure can be recorded for more than one compartment. For example, SARS-CoV-2 can be measured in people (humans), water, surface, or air. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (dataTypes). The data type for a part. Data types used in the ODM include: varchar, booleen, float, category, date, time, datetime, url, email. dataType corresponds the the entry or cell within a data table, most commonly within a report table. If the data entry has a unit, then the dataType corresponds to the unit and the dataType refers to ‘unit’. If the data entry is a category, then the dataType refers to ‘category’. All categories are varchar. Otherwise the dataType is identifed within the part entry. TBA: dataType for dictionary. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (dictionarySupport). Additional sheets for the Excel version of the ODM dictionary. Sheets or tabs for the ODM Excel dictionary include: all ERD tables (look-up tables and data entry tables) and additional supportig tables. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (domains). There are three domain types: biologic (i.e. Covid-19, chemical (i.e. nitrogen), physical measure (temperature). Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (exceptions). An exception part type for use in creating wide names that do not follow the general structure. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (groups). A collection of related measures. Used primary to group measurements and methods, this helps pare down the drop down list for a given measurement or methods. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (measurements). The attribute to describe a part type of measures. All measures have partType = “measure”. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (methods). Procedures or steps for collecting samples or performing measures. For example, methodExtract is a method that describes the how a sample was extracted. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (missingness). The part type for missingness values. Only used for the dictionary entries of parts. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (missingnessSets). Set of missingness values. Examples of missingness sets may include NR or NA esclusive sets, or general all-purpose sets. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (mmaSets). A set of categories. For example, site type has a list of different sites, such as a wastewater treatment plant, a septic tank, or a pumping station. Only used for the dictionary entries of parts. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (nomenclatures). A classification system to report the measure class. See partID = nomenclatureID. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (partTypes). Part types describe the purpose or use of the part. Enivornment data has three main part types: measure (i.e. covN1 viral measures, wasteawater flow rate, temperature), method (e.g. how the measure was taken), and attribute (such as a site name). See description of each of the part types within setID = partTypeCatSets. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (qualityIndicators). A measure of the quality of a reported value or sample. Only used for the dictionary entries of parts. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (qualityIndSets). Sets of quality indicators or measures. For example, PCR have a quality measure set. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (specimens). Measures or observations are taken from three types of substances: populations (humans or geographic areas), samples, sites. See partID = specimentID. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (specimenSets). Sets of specimens. Specimen sets are used when a measure or attribute can be recorded for more than one specimen. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (tables). Tables are where measures, methods and attributes are recorded. Tables represent the main entities of the environmental surveillance. An example of a table is site a collection of attributes such as site name and address to describe where environment samples are taken. PHES-ODM has report tables, but users can create their own tables as well. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (units). The unit of the measurement. Every measurement must have a unit. Meaning, units are a mandatory field whenever a measurement is recorded. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (unitSets). Sets of units. Contains units that are associated with part types such as measures. Sets are lists of input values. Each input value within a set is a part (has a partID) that can be reused between sets. For example, a set A could contain the values of ‘yes’ and ‘no’; and set B could contain the values of ‘yes’, ‘no’, and ‘maybe.’ partTypes with sets include aggregations, compartments, missingness, quality flags, specimens, and units. Measures with categories and dataTypes have their own specific sets (catSetID) because their input values are unique and are not reused. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.

It is one of four orthoebolaviruses known to cause illness in people, with only one confirmed human infection ever recorded. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (bundibugyoV). The species Bundibugyo ebolavirus is the taxonomic home of one virus, Bundibugyo virus (BDBV), that forms filamentous virions and is closely related to the Zaire ebolaviruses (EBOV). The virus is one of several that can cause Ebola disease in humans, taking the form of viral hemorrhagic fever. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (EVD). Ebola, also known as Ebola virus disease (EVD) and Ebola hemorrhagic fever (EHF), is a zoonotic viral hemorrhagic fever in humans and other primates, caused by four of the six known ebolaviruses. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (hfrs). Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a hemorrhagic fever caused by hantavirus infection. Symptoms usually occur 2 weeks after exposure to the hantavirus and come in five distinct clinical stages: febrile (toxic), hypotensive, low urine production (oliguric), high urine production (diuretic), and recovery. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (hps). Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), also called hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), is a severe respiratory disease caused by hantavirus infection. The main features of illness are microvascular leakage and acute respiratory distress syndrome. Symptoms occur anywhere from one to eight weeks after exposure to the virus and come in three distinct phases. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (snv). Sin Nombre virus (SNV) is the most common cause of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) in North America. Sin Nombre virus is transmitted mainly by the western deer mouse (Peromyscus sonoriensis). Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (htnv). Hantaan virus (HTNV) is the main cause of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in East Asia. Hantaan virus is transmitted by the striped field mouse (Apodemus agrarius). Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (seov). Seoul virus (SEOV) is one of the main causes of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS). Seoul virus is transmitted by the brown rat (Rattus norvegicus) and the black rat (Rattus rattus). Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (puuv). Puumala virus (PUUV) is the main cause of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in Europe and Russia. Puumala virus is transmitted by the bank vole (Clethrionomys glareolus). Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (dobv). Dobrava-Belgrade virus (DOBV) is the main cause of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in southern Europe. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (aivA). Measures of Aichivirus A, the species of aichivirus in the Kobuvirus genus, and picornavirus family. Typically a cause of gastrorenteritis in human or animal hosts. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (aivB). Measures of Aichivirus B, the species of aichivirus in the Kobuvirus genus, and picornavirus family. Typically a cause of gastrorenteritis in human or animal hosts. Also called Bovine kobuvirus. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (aivC). Measures of Aichivirus C, the species of aichivirus in the Kobuvirus genus, and picornavirus family. Typically a cause of gastrorenteritis in human or animal hosts. Also called Porcine kobuvirus. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (aivD). Measures of Aichivirus D, the species of aichivirus in the Kobuvirus genus, and picornavirus family. Typically a cause of gastrorenteritis in human or animal hosts. Also called kagovirus from black cattle. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (aivE). Measures of Aichivirus E, the species of aichivirus in the Kobuvirus genus, and picornavirus family. Typically a cause of gastrorenteritis in human or animal hosts. Also called Rabbit picornavirus. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (aivF). Measures of Aichivirus F, the species of aichivirus in the Kobuvirus genus, and picornavirus family. Typically a cause of gastrorenteritis in human or animal hosts. Also called bat kobuvirus. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (hAiV). Viral strain of Aichivirus A known to infect humans, typically of three known genotypes: A, B, or C. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (aivP1). A gene target for aichivirus, it is the genomic segment that encodes the structural viral capsid proteins forming the outer shell of the Aichivirus. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (hAiVGA). Viral strain of Aichivirus A known to infect humans of genotypes A. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (hAiVGB). Viral strain of Aichivirus A known to infect humans of genotypes B. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (hAiVGC). Viral strain of Aichivirus A known to infect humans of genotypes C. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (bocaparvo). Bocaparvovirus is a genus of viruses in the subfamily Parvovirinae of the virus family Parvoviridae. Humans, cattle, and dogs serve as natural hosts. There are 36 species in this genus. Diseases associated with this genus include, in humans, acute respiratory illness, and in cattle, diarrhea and mild respiratory symptoms. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (hbov). Human bocavirus (HBoV) is the name given to all viruses in the genus Bocaparvovirus of virus family Parvoviridae that are known to infect humans. Some of these viruses cause human disease. HBoV1 is strongly implicated in causing some cases of lower respiratory tract infection, especially in young children, and several of the viruses have been linked to gastroenteritis, although the full clinical role of this emerging infectious disease remains to be elucidated. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (cacipacore). Orthoflavivirus cacipacoreense, causitive agent of the rare Cacipacore virus Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (pcv1). Porcine Circoviruses (PCV) are the smallest viruses replicating autonomously in eukaryotic cells. The virions are non-enveloped and spherical with a diameter of 16-18 nm and the covalently closed and single-stranded DNA genomes comprise less than 1800 nucleotides. Porcine circovirus type 1 (PCV1) is not linked with a disease. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (pcv2). Porcine Circoviruses (PCV) are the smallest viruses replicating autonomously in eukaryotic cells. The virions are non-enveloped and spherical with a diameter of 16-18 nm and the covalently closed and single-stranded DNA genomes comprise less than 1800 nucleotides. Porcine circovirus type 2 (PCV2) is the etiological agent of Postweaning Multisystemic Wasting Syndrome (PMWS), a new emerging and multifactorial disease in swine. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (cosaV). Cosavirus is a genus of viruses in the order Picornavirales, in the family Picornaviridae. Human serve as natural hosts. There are 5 species od enteric viruses in this genus. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (deltaretro). Deltaretrovirus is a genus of the Retroviridae family. It consists of exogenous horizontally transmitted viruses found in several groups of mammals. This genus of viruses is known for its propensity to target immune cells and oncogenicity. Infection is usually asymptomatic, but inflammation and cancer can develop over time. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (priTlym1). Human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1, Primate T-lymphotropic virus 1, or human T-lymphotropic virus (HTLV-I or HTLV-1), also called the adult T-cell lymphoma virus type 1, is a deltaretrovirus of the human T-lymphotropic virus (HTLV) family. Latin species name: Deltaretrovirus priTlym1. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (priTlym2). Human T-cell lymphotropic virus 2, or Primate T-lymphotropic virus 2 (HTLV-II or HTLV-2), is a deltaretrovirus of the human T-lymphotropic virus (HTLV) family. Latin species name: Deltaretrovirus priTlym2. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (eeev). Eastern equine encephalitis virus (EEEV) is defined as a neurotropic alphavirus that causes severe disease in horses, characterized by high mortality rates and pathological lesions in the central nervous system, including inflammation and infiltration of immune cells. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (erythroparvo). Erythroparvovirus is defined as a small DNA virus that belongs to the Parvoviridae family, known for causing various illnesses, including fifth disease, arthritis, and anemia, particularly in immunocompromised individuals. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (hParvB19V). Human parvovirus B19 is defined as a nonenveloped, single-stranded DNA virus belonging to the Erythrovirus genus of the Parvoviridae family, which primarily infects humans and can cause a variety of syndromes, including erythema infectiosum, arthropathy, and complications such as aplastic anemia and fetal hydrops. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (gDuodenalis). A protozoan parasite that causes anthroponotic or zoonotic diarrheal disease which can be opportunistic or affect healthy, immunocompetent individuals. Giardia duodenalis is the one commonly described type of Giardia, that is found in mammals including humans. This species complex comprise eight assemblages Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (g18s). The 18S ribosomal RNA (18S rRNA) gene in Giardia is a primary genetic target used for detecting, identifying, and classifying the microscopic intestinal parasite responsible for giardiasis. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (gammaretro). Gammaretrovirus is a genus in the Retroviridae family. Example species are the murine leukemia virus and the feline leukemia virus. They cause various sarcomas, leukemias and immune deficiencies in mammals, reptiles and birds. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (lymphocrypto). Lymphocryptovirus is a genus of viruses in the order Herpesvirales, in the family Orthoherpesviridae, in the subfamily Gammaherpesvirinae. This genus includes the human-infecting Epstein–Barr virus, as well as viruses that infect both Old World monkeys and New World monkeys. Also called gamma-1 herpesviruses, there are nine species in this genus. Diseases associated with this genus include: mononucleosis, Burkitt’s lymphoma, and nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (hadv). Human mastadenoviruses (HAdVs) are non-enveloped, double-stranded icosahedral DNA viruses, approximately 90–100 nm in diameter, with fibre projections on each of the 12 vertices. The genome is approximately 30–35 kilobases in length and encodes more than 30 structural and non-structural proteins. HAdV belongs to the genus Mastadenovirus, one of five genera within the Adenoviridae family. Within Mastadenovirus, seven known groups have been identified (A-G), which can be further classified into 54 serotypes. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (hadvA). Group A of the human mastadenovirus genus (HAdV-A). Includes serotypes 12, 18, and 31. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (hadvB). Group B of the human mastadenovirus genus (HAdV-B). Includes serotypes 3, and 16. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (hadvC). Group C of the human mastadenovirus genus (HAdV-C). Includes serotypes 1, 2, 5, and 6. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (hadvD). Group D of the human mastadenovirus genus (HAdV-D). Includes serotypes 8, 17, 19, 23, 36, 51, and 58. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (hadvE). Group E of the human mastadenovirus genus (HAdV-E). Includes serotype 4. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (hadvF). Group F of the human mastadenovirus genus (HAdV-F). Includes serotypes 40 and 41. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (hpev). Human parechovirus (HPeV; family Picornaviridae, genus Parechovirus) is a nonenveloped virus with a positive-sense single-stranded RNA genome that infects humans. HPeV strains are currently subdivided into 16 genotypes (i.e., HPeV1 to HPeV16), and HPeV1 and HPeV3 are the genotypes mostly causing gastroenteritis, respiratory syndrome, and febrile illness mainly in young children. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (hpev1). Human parechovirus (HPeV) of the genotype 1 (HPeV1), capable of causing gastroenteritis, respiratory syndrome, and febrile illness in humans. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (picobirna). The single genus of the Picobirnaviridae family, Picobirnavirus, members of which have been identified in the feces of humans, rabbits, and a variety of other species of mammals, reptiles, and birds. Picobirnaviruses have been increasingly recognized with the advent of deep sequencing analysis of fecal specimens from many species of animals, and distinct genetic subgroups are now described. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (pyv). Studies reported human Polyomaviruses (PyV) (mainly strains BK and JC) contaminating water and food. These strains are, respectively, associated with nephropathy and progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy. Others link them to common respiratory illnesses. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (pyvJC). JCPyV, or human polyomavirus JC, is defined a polyomavirus and an etiological agent associated with progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, characterized by demyelination in the central nervous system, and has been detected in certain tumors, suggesting a potential but unproven link to cancer development. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (pyvBK). BKPyV, or human polyomavirus BK, is defined a polyomavirus and an etiological agent associated with nephropathy. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (hhv6). Roseolovirus refers to a group of viruses, including HHV-6A and HHV-6B, that are characterized by their ability to cause various diseases, persist in latency within different cell types, and integrate into the human genome. Their detection does not necessarily indicate causation of disease, highlighting the need for careful interpretation of diagnostic results within clinical contexts. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (hhv6A). HHV-6A is a roseolovirus that has been described as more neurovirulent, and as such is more frequently found in patients with neuroinflammatory diseases such as multiple sclerosis. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (hhv6B). HHV-6B is a roseolovirus and the cause of the common childhood illness exanthema subitum (also known as roseola infantum or sixth disease). It is passed on from child to child. It is uncommon for adults to contract this disease as most people have had it by kindergarten, and once contracted, immunity arises and prevents future reinfection. Additionally, HHV-6B reactivation is common in transplant recipients, which can cause several clinical manifestations such as encephalitis, bone marrow suppression, and pneumonitis. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (saliA). Salivirus A (Salivirus aklasse) has been identified in humans and chimpanzees and may cause acute gastroenteritis in humans, having been detected in 0% to 8.7% of fecal samples collected from gastroenteritis in different human populations. Salivirus is ubiquitous in wastewater of human origin and river water specimens worldwide and represents a potential indicator human RNA virus for monitoring of environmental samples. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (safv). Saffold virus (SAFV) is an emerging human cardiovirus associated with respiratory and gastrointestinal infection, and, more recently, to symptoms related to the endocrine, cardiovascular, and neurological systems. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (safv1). Strain 1 of the saffold virus (SAFV-1). The only strain with global distribution. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (safv2). Strain 2 of the saffold virus (SAFV-2) Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (safv3). Strain 3 of the saffold virus (SAFV-3) Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (safv4). Strain 4 of the saffold virus (SAFV-4) Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (safv5). Strain 5 of the saffold virus (SAFV-5) Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (safv6). Strain 6 of the saffold virus (SAFV-6) Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (safv7). Strain 7 of the saffold virus (SAFV-7) Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (safv8). Strain 8 of the saffold virus (SAFV-8) Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (tanapox). Tanapox (a virus from the genus Yatapoxvirus) was first seen among individuals in the flood plain of the Tana River in Kenya during two epidemics (1957 and 1962) of acute febrile illness accompanied by localized skin lesions. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (ttv). Torque teno virus (TTV) is the type species in the genus Anellovirus. The viruses are small (30–50 nm) and non-enveloped with a circular single-stranded DNA genome that is approximately 3.8 kb in size. More than 90% of adults worldwide are said to be infected with TTV. The viruses have not been conclusively shown to cause disease in humans, although they have been associated with some acute respiratory illnesses in infants. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (hpev3). Human parechovirus (HPeV) of the genotype 3 (HPeV3), capable of causing gastroenteritis, respiratory syndrome, and febrile illness in humans. Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.

title: Sets
text:
NA
(methods). Procedures or steps for collecting samples or performing measures. For example, methodExtract is a method that describes the how a sample was extracted. met


NA (amrSoft). Software use to analyse bacterial genomes and genes for anti-mocrobial resistance (AMR). Status: active. First released: 3.0.0. Last updated: 3.0.0.


NA (bactMeth). Description of the bacterial testing/detection method. Status: active. First released: 3.0.0. Last updated: 3.0.0.


NA (cladeAn). Software tool or pipeline for determining the clade or lineage of an organism. Status: active. First released: 3.0.0. Last updated: 3.0.0.


NA (conSeqSoft). Software use to run consensus sequence on sequencing analyses. Status: active. First released: 3.0.0. Last updated: 3.0.0.


NA (dedup). Sequencing and PCR deduplication method. Status: active. First released: 3.0.0. Last updated: 3.0.0.


NA (dehost). Sequencing and PCR dehosting method. Status: active. First released: 3.0.0. Last updated: 3.0.0.


NA (extBlank). Binary Y/N indicator for if extraction blank was used as a control for the nucleic acid extraction process. Status: active. First released: 2.2.0. Last updated: 2.2.0.


NA (extraction). Description of the nucleic acid extraction method. Status: active. First released: 1.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (gte). The molecular technique used to selectively capture and amplify specific regions of interest from a genome. Status: active. First released: 3.0.0. Last updated: 3.0.0.


NA (inhibMeth). Description of the method used to evaluate molecular inhibition. Status: active. First released: 1.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (libraryKit). The name of the DNA/RNA library preparation kit used to generate the library being sequenced. Status: active. First released: 3.0.0. Last updated: 3.0.0.


NA (methodConc). Description of the method to concentrate a wastewater sample. Status: active. First released: 1.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (pasteur). Binary indicator for whether a sample was pasteurized as part of its processing. Status: active. First released: 2.2.0. Last updated: 2.2.0.


NA (pcrAct). Describes a given PCR cycle for delineating more method information. Status: active. First released: 2.2.0. Last updated: 2.2.0.


NA (pcrmeth). Description of the PCR method. Status: active. First released: 1.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (popAs). Method for assessing the population count for a site/polygon. Status: active. First released: 3.0.0. Last updated: 3.0.0.


NA (primer). Method ID used for indicating the primer used for a PCR or sequencing assay. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (qaqc). Quality assurance and quality control method. Status: depreciated. First released: 1.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (qcMethod). Method for sequencing quality control or assessment. Status: active. First released: 3.0.0. Last updated: 3.0.0.


NA (rawSeqProc). The software/library/pipeline used to process the raw sequencing data. Status: active. First released: 3.0.0. Last updated: 3.0.0.


NA (readMapper). The name of the bioinformatics software tool used to align short DNA or RNA sequence reads (obtained from high-throughput sequencing technologies like Illumina, PacBio, or Oxford Nanopore) to a reference genome or transcriptome. Status: active. First released: 3.0.0. Last updated: 3.0.0.


NA (resuspension). Describes the method used for resuspending material. Status: active. First released: 2.2.0. Last updated: 2.2.0.


NA (retainedElement). The element retained after centrifugation, filtration, solid separation, etc. Status: active. First released: 2.2.0. Last updated: 2.2.0.


NA (sampleTypeOther). Description for other type of method not listed in collection. depreciated. Status: depreciated. First released: 1.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (scriptVersion). Used to specify the script or script version used to extract summary information (i.e. coverage and mutation frequency statistics, etc.) from the sequencing output. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (seqAss). The name of the software/toolkit/pipeline used for assembling sequences from reads. Status: active. First released: 3.0.0. Last updated: 3.0.0.


NA (seqLay). The layout of genetic material used in sequencing. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (seqQC). The quality control pipeline for sequencing or PCR data. Status: active. First released: 3.0.0. Last updated: 3.0.0.


NA (seqSel). The primer sequence selection method used in sequencing. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (seqStrat). The sequencing strategy used for an analysis. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (seroMeth). The method used to determine the serovar. Status: active. First released: 3.0.0. Last updated: 3.0.0.


NA (shipOnIce). Was the sample kept cool while being shipped to the lab Status: active. First released: 1.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (solidSep). Process used to separate solid and liquid phases of the sample. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (spikeMat). Material into which the recovery efficiency control target is spiked. Status: active. First released: 1.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (spikeTarget). Method specifying the recovery efficiency control target. This matches on to the the spike material method ID. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (stdCurveMet). Describes the specific approach used for calculating a standard curve. Status: active. First released: 2.2.0. Last updated: 2.2.0.


NA (stoMed). The medium used to store a sample before final analysis. Status: active. First released: 3.0.0. Last updated: 3.0.0.


NA (tempType). Specifies whether a PCR or sequencing used RNA or DNA as the template for the reaction. Status: active. First released: 2.2.0. Last updated: 2.2.0.


NA (tyOtDep). Description for other type of sample not listed in Status: depreciated. First released: 1.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.

title: Sets
text:
NA
(missingness). The part type for missingness values. Only used for the dictionary entries of parts.



NA (dnc). A missingness value for when when data was not measured or collected; an analysis not run, etc. Status: active. First released: 3.0.0. Last updated: 3.0.0.


NA (miss). A general missingness value for missing data, used when data is not included for an unknown reason. Status: active. First released: 3.0.0. Last updated: 3.0.0.


NA (NA). The field for which the expected value is not a property of the described object. Status: active. First released: 1.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (nan). The outcome of a measurement is not a valid number (plus or minus infinity, error, …) Status: active. First released: 1.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (nr). A value could have been recorded, however, it was not. Status: active. First released: 1.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (NULL). A logical representation of a statement that is neither TRUE nor FALSE. Status: active. First released: 1.0.0. Last updated: 3.0.0.


NA (restrict). Missing data is witheld because it is restricted access. Status: active. First released: 3.0.0. Last updated: 3.0.0.


NA (undisc). A value has been recorded, however it was not included in the dataset. Status: active. First released: 1.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.

title: Sets
text:
NA
(missingnessSets). Set of missingness values. Examples of missingness sets may include NR or NA esclusive sets, or general all-purpose sets.



NA (genMissingnessSet). The general set for missingness values. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (nrNAMissingnessSet). Not reported, Not applicable missing set. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (geoRefMissingnessSet). A missingness set for field populated by the geographical reference tables (countries, zones) Status: active. First released: 3.0.1. Last updated: 3.0.1.

title: Sets
text:
NA
(mmaSets). A set of categories. For example, site type has a list of different sites, such as a wastewater treatment plant, a septic tank, or a pumping station. Only used for the dictionary entries of parts.



NA (actionTypeSet). A set of valid categories for the public health action type field. Status: active. First released: 3.0.0. Last updated: 3.0.0.


NA (allActionsSet). A set of all valid categories for public health action, regardless of action type. Status: active. First released: 3.0.0. Last updated: 3.0.0.


NA (allStandardSet). Set of valid input values for the standard field. Status: active. First released: 3.0.0. Last updated: 3.0.0.


NA (amrClassSet). A set of valid categories for the public health action field, where the action type is ‘antimicrobial resistance (AMR) classification’. Status: active. First released: 3.0.0. Last updated: 3.0.0.


NA (amrSoftSet). The valid set of AMR analysis software categories. Status: active. First released: 3.0.0. Last updated: 3.0.0.

title: Sets
text:
NA
(partTypes). Part types describe the purpose or use of the part. Enivornment data has three main part types: measure (i.e. covN1 viral measures, wasteawater flow rate, temperature), method (e.g. how the measure was taken), and attribute (such as a site name). See description of each of the part types within setID = partTypeCatSets.



NA (partTypes). Part types describe the purpose or use of the part. Enivornment data has three main part types: measure (i.e. covN1 viral measures, wasteawater flow rate, temperature), method (e.g. how the measure was taken), and attribute (such as a site name). See description of each of the part types within setID = partTypeCatSets. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (shortName). Shortened names for tables and other important parts for use in wide names. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 3.0.0.


NA (aggregations). Statistical measures used to report a measure. Each measure reported as a number should be reported with an aggregation. The default aggregation is sin, which corresponds to a single measurement. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (aggregationScales). The scale of an aggregation set. Aggregation scales include quantitative and qualitative. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (attributes). Attributes describe the who, where, when, and why of environmental surveillance. There are attributes for domain, specimen, compartment, or table. Attributes are one of the three main components or ways to report environment surviellence data. The other two components are measures and methods. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (aggregationSets). Sets of aggregations. Examples of aggregation sets include logarithm, linear and boolean. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (categories). A discrete list of values that can be reported for a measure, method or attribute. A use-case example of categories would be how they are used to record the site where a measure is taken (partID = geoType). For the geoType attribute there are different type of sites where samples can be taken: a wastwater treatment plant, airplane holding tank, wastwater pumping station, etc. Each of these site types is recorded as a category that can be identified in categorySetID = sTypeCatSets Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (classes). A class is a collection of one or more related measures or methods within a group. A group can have one more more classes to describe different parts or the class. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (compartments). The substance from which a sample was taken. For example, wastewater has component of “water”. Compartments are attributes of measures, methods, units, and aggregations. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (compartmentSets). Sets of compartments. Compartment sets are used to identify when a measure can be recorded for more than one compartment. For example, SARS-CoV-2 can be measured in people (humans), water, surface, or air. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (dataTypes). The data type for a part. Data types used in the ODM include: varchar, booleen, float, category, date, time, datetime, url, email. dataType corresponds the the entry or cell within a data table, most commonly within a report table. If the data entry has a unit, then the dataType corresponds to the unit and the dataType refers to ‘unit’. If the data entry is a category, then the dataType refers to ‘category’. All categories are varchar. Otherwise the dataType is identifed within the part entry. TBA: dataType for dictionary. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 3.0.1.


NA (dictionarySupport). Additional sheets for the Excel version of the ODM dictionary. Sheets or tabs for the ODM Excel dictionary include: all ERD tables (look-up tables and data entry tables) and additional supportig tables. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (dictSets). Sets used to describe and group dictionary tables. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (domains). There are three domain types: biologic (i.e. Covid-19, chemical (i.e. nitrogen), physical measure (temperature). Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (exceptions). An exception part type for use in creating wide names that do not follow the general structure. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (groups). A collection of related measures. Used primary to group measurements and methods, this helps pare down the drop down list for a given measurement or methods. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (measurements). The attribute to describe a part type of measures. All measures have partType = “measure”. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (methods). Procedures or steps for collecting samples or performing measures. For example, methodExtract is a method that describes the how a sample was extracted. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (missingness). The part type for missingness values. Only used for the dictionary entries of parts. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (missingnessSets). Set of missingness values. Examples of missingness sets may include NR or NA esclusive sets, or general all-purpose sets. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (mmaSets). A set of categories. For example, site type has a list of different sites, such as a wastewater treatment plant, a septic tank, or a pumping station. Only used for the dictionary entries of parts. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (nomenclatures). A classification system to report the measure class. See partID = nomenclatureID. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (partSupport). Parts designed to support the metadata definition of other parts in the parts table. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (qualityIndicators). A measure of the quality of a reported value or sample. Only used for the dictionary entries of parts. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (qualityIndSets). Sets of quality indicators or measures. For example, PCR have a quality measure set. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (shortSets). Sets used to group together short names for tables or part types in ODM. Status: active. First released: 3.0.0. Last updated: 3.0.0.


NA (specimens). Measures or observations are taken from three types of substances: populations (humans or geographic areas), samples, sites. See partID = specimentID. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (specimenSets). Sets of specimens. Specimen sets are used when a measure or attribute can be recorded for more than one specimen. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (tables). Tables are where measures, methods and attributes are recorded. Tables represent the main entities of the environmental surveillance. An example of a table is site a collection of attributes such as site name and address to describe where environment samples are taken. PHES-ODM has report tables, but users can create their own tables as well. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (tableSupport). Parts designed to support the metadata definition oftables in the parts table. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (units). The unit of the measurement. Every measurement must have a unit. Meaning, units are a mandatory field whenever a measurement is recorded. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (unitSets). Sets of units. Contains units that are associated with part types such as measures. Sets are lists of input values. Each input value within a set is a part (has a partID) that can be reused between sets. For example, a set A could contain the values of ‘yes’ and ‘no’; and set B could contain the values of ‘yes’, ‘no’, and ‘maybe.’ partTypes with sets include aggregations, compartments, missingness, quality flags, specimens, and units. Measures with categories and dataTypes have their own specific sets (catSetID) because their input values are unique and are not reused. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.

title: Sets
text:
NA
(qualityIndicators). A measure of the quality of a reported value or sample. Only used for the dictionary entries of parts.



NA (ampliArtifact). Sequence amplification artifacts detected. Status: active. First released: 2.3.0. Last updated: 2.3.0.


NA (beLOD). Measure is below the limit of detection (LOD) for a specific analyte. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (belowLOQ). Indicates that a measurement detected the analyte, but at levels below the limit of quantification (LOQ). Status: active. First released: 2.2.3. Last updated: 2.2.3.


NA (delayArriv). A substantial delay (ie. of more than 14 days) between sample collection and the start of analysis. Status: active. First released: 2.2.3. Last updated: 2.2.3.


NA (expFail). PCR experiment failed. No value reported. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (flagAI). The original sample was inhibited; however, the inhibition has been addressed through dilution. The reported concentration estimate is the updated result after addressing inhibition. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (flagB). Analytical result may be subject to “trace” levels of contamination; the target analyte was also detected in negative controls on the same run as the sample. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (flagFI). The original sample was inhibited; however, the inhibition has not been successfully addressed. Therefore, no concentration estimate has been reported. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (flagJ). Analytical result falls below the lowest concentration of the experiment-specific standard curve but above the y-intercept value; the reported value is based on the extrapolation of the standard curve in the non-linear region. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (flagND). No amplification occurred in the reaction; non-detect. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (flagUJ). Observed quantitation cycle is greater than the experiment-specific standard curve intercept value but evidence of clear amplification was present (i.e., “trace” signal observed); the reported value is based on the extrapolation of the standard curve in the non-linear region. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (flagUQ). Unquantifiable, Ct value exceeds the maximum value of the standard curve. There was a detect, but we cannot quantify it with certainty. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (frozen). Sample was frozen before analysis or processing Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (lAGC). Average coverage of the genome is low/poor. Status: active. First released: 2.3.0. Last updated: 2.3.0.


NA (lBC). The percentage of the genome covered by reads (the breadth) is low. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (lDC). Poor coverage, specifically an insufficient number of reads or too many sequencing reads that are mapped incorrectly. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (leaked). Sample leaked, some volume and material was lost. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (lowCovMut). Low coverage of characteristic mutations. Status: active. First released: 2.3.0. Last updated: 2.3.0.


NA (lowQualSeq). Low-quality sequence. Status: active. First released: 2.3.0. Last updated: 2.3.0.


NA (lowSNRatio). Low signal-to-noise ratio. Status: active. First released: 2.3.0. Last updated: 2.3.0.


NA (lowVol). Sample is low-volume, but was run regardless. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (lPGC). Only captured a small/low percentage of the genome. Status: active. First released: 2.3.0. Last updated: 2.3.0.


NA (mI). Multiple issues have arisen in the sequencing process. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (noConcern). A flag to indicate there is are no quality concern about the measure or sample. Status: active. First released: 1.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (noLabel). Sample had no label Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (noTime). Sample is missing the autosampler time; incomplete metadata on collection. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (ntcAmp). Quality flag for when the non-template control (NTC) still sees amplification - ie. The NTCs in qPCR show a Ct value less than 40, or NTCs in a ddPCR have 3 or more positive droplets. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 3.0.0.


NA (ntcFlag). quality indicator for when there is observed amplicifation in the non-template controls (NTCs) of a PCR reaction. Status: depreciated. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 3.0.0.


NA (oor). Value is outside of the allowable range for quality control. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (out). Value is an outlier and may be of questionable quality. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (qf1). A flag to indicate there is a quality concern, not otherwise sepcified. Status: active. First released: 1.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (sC). Sequencing shows sparse coverage, ie. numerical breadth of coverage shows as adequate but coverage plots reveal missing genome pieces. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (seqContam). Sequence is contaminated. Status: active. First released: 2.3.0. Last updated: 2.3.0.


NA (shortRead). Read lengths are shorter than expected. Status: active. First released: 2.3.0. Last updated: 2.3.0.


NA (spill). Sample contents spilled from container. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (wI). The 95% interval is too wide, low confidence in results. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (wrongStorage). Sample was stored inappropriately. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (wrongTemp). Sample was stored at an inappropriate temperature. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.

title: Sets
text:
NA
(tables). Tables are where measures, methods and attributes are recorded. Tables represent the main entities of the environmental surveillance. An example of a table is site a collection of attributes such as site name and address to describe where environment samples are taken. PHES-ODM has report tables, but users can create their own tables as well.



NA (accessions). Table for recording accession IDs for external data, namely sequences in large sequencing databases and repositories. The short name for the table (partID) can be found in the instructions field. Status: active. First released: 2.3.0. Last updated: 2.3.0.


NA (addresses). The table that contains information about addresses. Addresses can recorded for sites, organizations or contacts (indivduals). The Sites, Organizations, and Contacts tables include a link to the addresses table through Address ID. The short name for the table (partID) can be found in the instructions field. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (calculations). Table for recording data on data treatments and calculations applied to measurements and reported values. Status: active. First released: 2.3.0. Last updated: 2.3.0.


NA (contacts). The table that contains information about a contact; a person who is the contact of a site or laboratory. The short name for the table (partID) can be found in the instructions field. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (countries). Look up table for the possible country inputs. The short name for the table (partID) can be found in the instructions field. Status: active. First released: 2.1.0. Last updated: 2.1.0.


NA (datasets). A report table for capturing details about data’s parental data set and data custodians. Supplying attribution for data collectors. The short name for the table (partID) can be found in the instructions field. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.

NA (measureSets). The table that identifies sets of measures. Examples of measure sets include a set of replicates, dilutions (used to generate a Ct curve) or varients that are identified in a single sample. The short name for the table (partID) can be found in the instructions field. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.


NA (organizations). The table that contains information about a laboratory. The short name for the table (partID) can be found in the instructions field. Status: active. First released: 1.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.

Protocols are a group of related protocol steps. For example a protocol step can describe a sample concentration, extraction, inhibition or a measurement. Protocols can include both methodID (a proceedure) and measureIDs (a measure). An example of a method is centrifugation; where the centriguation rotation speed is described as a measure. The short name for the table (partID) can be found in the instructions field. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.

The short name for the table (partID) can be found in the instructions field. Status: active. First released: 2.0.0. Last updated: 2.0.0.

A sample is defined as a representative volume of wastewater (or other forms of water or liquid), air, or surface area taken from a site.Samples can be combined, split, stored and reused. title: Sets
text:
NA
(unitSets). Sets of units. Contains units that are associated with part types such as measures. Sets are lists of input values. Each input value within a set is a part (has a partID) that can be reused between sets. For example, a set A could contain the values of ‘yes’ and ‘no’; and set B could contain the values of ‘yes’, ‘no’, and ‘maybe.’ partTypes with sets include aggregations, compartments, missingness, quality flags, specimens, and units. Measures with categories and dataTypes have their own specific sets (catSetID) because their input values are unique and are not reused.

title: Tables
text:
Table types
Dictionary v3.0.1 Documentation v2.1.1
The ODM database model has 26 tables in its full relational database, with 19 tables for reporting data, and 7 look-up or reference tables. Of these report tables, only 3 are mandatory for the simplest micro-report template. In addition to many of the tables being optional, each table also has a mix of mandatory and optional headers. The full model is commonly referred to as “long” tables as it stores data with one measurement per row, though wide versions are also possible (see section on wide names).
There are three general table types, which can be further thematically categorized:
1) Results tables. These are the main tables of interest for environmental surveillance reporting, which store information on samples and on the results of analysis of samples. Tables in this category include the measures and samples tables, which are used for regular reporting of new measurements and information on sample collection. There are three additional results tables that support regular reporting, but that are optional: - measureSets (optional) is used to link measures, - sampleRelationships (optional) is used when samples are pooled or split, and - qualityReports (optional) is used for detailed quality assurance and control measures.
2) Program description tables. Tables in this category store administrative information about the organizations involved in testing, locations where tests were conducted, protocols used, etc. These are tables that are updated much more infrequently than results tables. These can be further divided into:
3) Dictionary reference tables. The parts table describes all elements of the ODM, including tables, table headers, measures, methods, categories, and units. The sets table stores collections of parts, such as units grouped together in a unitSet. The languages and translations tables support translations for the parts and sets tables. The countries and zones tables standardize location information to the ISO-2 and ISO-3 to reduce ambiguity and free-text errors when populating these fields, while improving interoperability of location metadata. wideNames is used for recording “wide names” (ie. variables or table headers for “wide” format data) in current use across various PHES-ODM templates, and has built in code to assist users in generating their own ODM-compatible “wide names”.

title: Tables
text:
Contact information tables. The organizations, contacts, and addresses tables store contact information for the testing site and/or the person who performed the testing.
Protocol or methods tables. The protocols and instruments tables hold information on the methods used for sample collection or measurement. protocolSteps and protocolRelationships tables are used in conjunction with the protocols table.
Data source & processing tables. The accessions, datasets, and calculations tables record details about data provenance and ownership. accessions provides links to external datasets were either complimentary data (ie. sequencing ouptputs) or the original data may be found. The datasets table includes information on the data custodian and owner, as well as licensing.calculations records the kinds of calculations, models, or data treatments used to generate the data from raw inputs.
Geospatial tables. The polygons and sites tables stores information on the sample area. sites records details about the physical sampling site and its context, while polygons records geospatial data about the area the aa site may reflect - for example if the site is a wastewater treatment plant, the polygon would reflect the treatment plant’s catchment area. The polygonRelationships table is used in conjunction with the polygons table.

title: Tables
text:
Header roles
Each table in the PHES-ODM has column headers, also known as table variables, fields, or entity relationship attributes. The header serves as the top row and contains the variable name.
Primary key (PK) - All tables have one primary key. The primary key serves as a unique identifier for each row in the table, meaning that a primary key value cannot be repeated.
Foreign key (FK) - Tables may have one or more foreign keys. A foreign key is when a primary key being referenced in another table, connecting an entry in one table to an entry in another table. This allows for relationships to be established between tables, making it possible to link data between different tables.
Header (header) - This label is used in a table description when a header is not a primary or foreign key.

title: Tables
text:
Mandatory, optional, mandatoryIf
Each header may be classified as either mandatory or optional. In the measures table, examples of mandatory headers are the measureID and aDateEnd. The PHES-ODM validation toolkit can be used to validate data, and will return an error if a table lacks a mandatory header or if there are missing row entries for mandatory fields.
Additionally, there are special headers called mandatoryIf headers. These headers are mandatory if certain conditions apply. For example, the protocol steps table has row entries that are either measures or methods. If the row entry is a measure, then a unit becomes mandatory since all measures must have a unit. Therefore, units are mandatoryIf in the protocol steps table.
